text.en: A great Indian thinker once said, it is the same India which has withstood the shocks of centuries, of hundreds of foreign invasions and of hundreds of upheavals of manners and customs. The 11th and 12th centuries were a time of change: new invaders from the northwest, new kingdoms, wonderful temples and great scholars. In this chapter we follow both the conflicts and the creativity of this period.

Across the northwest and all the way to Punjab ruled a powerful dynasty called the Hindu Shahis. After the battle in northern Punjab, in which Mahmud of Ghazni defeated them, he had easy access to the Indus plains and beyond. Mahmud of Ghazni was the first notable invader of India in this period. He raided several times, plundering temple treasures. At Somanatha in Gujarat, despite strong local resistance and severe losses to his army, he destroyed the Shiva temple and looted its great wealth. Writers of the time describe the violence of these raids. In another account Queen Naikidevi, mother of the young king Mularaja of Gujarat, led her army on horseback, with her son in her lap, and won a victory over such an invader.
Al-Biruni, a Persian scholar from Khwarizm in present-day Uzbekistan, came with Mahmud. He was a mathematician, astronomer, geographer, historian and linguist all in one. He learned Sanskrit, studied Indian science and religion and wrote a detailed book about India. He translated Patanjali's Yogasutras into Arabic. Bhaskaracharya, the great mathematician, wrote on arithmetic and algebra in his Lilavati. He had a gift for poetry and wrote in verse to make mathematics enjoyable, with riddles, such as one-eighth and one-ninth of one-eighth of a group sporting in a lotus pond.
The Cholas under Rajendra Chola extended their power. He conquered the northern part of Sri Lanka, including Anuradhapura, and what his inscriptions call the islands of the sea, which most historians identify with the Maldives. He built a new city and a great temple at Gangaikondacholapuram to commemorate his victory over northern rulers. His naval expedition across the sea, supported by Indian merchant guilds, was a punitive expedition and not an attempt to occupy. The Paramaras of Malwa under King Bhoja, a scholar-king who wrote on many subjects, began the impressive Bhojeshwar temple, which remains a marvel although never completed. After Bhoja's death in 1055 the Paramaras gradually declined. The Eastern Gangas started the Jagannatha temple at Puri and, in the mid-13th century, the grand Sun temple at Konark. In the Deccan the Western Chalukyas faded and the Kakatiyas and Hoysalas grew stronger. The Hoysalas' unique temple style has intricately carved stone pillars, sculptures and panels. Their founder Sala is said to have struck a tiger when a Jain ascetic cried Poy, Sala, which in old Kannada means strike, Sala. Prithviraja III of the Chahamana dynasty, known today as Prithviraj Chauhan, fought many battles with neighbouring kings.
Muhammad of Ghor, a Turkish ruler of Afghanistan, was a turning point. After wars in northern India, he left trusted generals behind when he returned. One was Qutb-ud-din Aibak, who later founded the Delhi Sultanate. Muhammad Ghuri was killed in 1206, the same year as his general Bakhtiyar Khilji was assassinated. On his way to Bengal Bakhtiyar Khilji destroyed large Buddhist monasteries and universities, such as Nalanda and Vikramashila. A Tibetan monk, Dharmasvamin, visiting some three decades later, found Nalanda half-ruined. Centres of learning like Nalanda were important for scholars from many lands, so their destruction was a great loss for education and culture. The Delhi Sultanate, which grew from this, will be studied in Grade 8.
Many poets, philosophers, saints and scientists belong to this period and their works still illuminate us. Basaveshwara, a minister at Kalyani in Karnataka, left his post to become a social and religious reformer, like other Bhakti saints who made spirituality more personal and accessible and broke down some social barriers. Neighbouring kingdoms often fought but also made alliances. On a few occasions local rulers came together to form a coalition against a foreign invader. The lesson of the period is resilience in the face of conflict, and the enduring power of knowledge, learning and creativity.

problem.en: Give two examples each of change and continuity in this period.

text.en: Change: new rulers from the northwest and the start of the Delhi Sultanate.
Change: destruction of centres such as Nalanda.
Continuity: temple building, Sanskrit scholarship and Bhakti traditions continued.

prompt.en: Why was Nalanda important and what happened to it?

requiredIdeas.en: It was a great centre of learning with thousands of scholars.
It was destroyed in the late 12th century.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking the whole period had only conflict.

points.en: Mahmud of Ghazni raided northwestern India and Somanatha.
Al-Biruni and Bhaskaracharya show the achievements of scholars.
Cholas, Paramaras, Eastern Gangas, Hoysalas built great temples.
The Ghurids led to the Delhi Sultanate; resilience and learning continued.
